issues.legal_issue: A building leased by a public body falls within an exemption from rent-control protections when the applicable statutory definition expressly includes buildings taken on lease by that body.
material_facts: The State leased the landlord’s premises to operate a training centre.
The landlord terminated the tenancy by notice and brought an ordinary civil suit to recover possession.
During the relevant period, the statutory definition of a public building included buildings taken on lease by the government, and the rent-control legislation exempted public buildings.
Later amendments restoring a narrower exemption were made effective only from a later date and did not apply to the relevant period.
issues.conclusion: The leased premises were exempt from the Rent Act during the relevant period, so the landlord could seek possession under the general law by filing a civil suit. The appeal was dismissed, and the contrary High Court decision was overruled.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(1)(a) and 3(o) of the Uttar Pradesh Public Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, as amended in 1976, must be given their plain and deliberately widened meaning: the exemption covered buildings leased by the government, not merely buildings it owned or let to others. The later amendments were effective from 18 May 1983 and were not retrospective to the relevant period. Section 20’s restriction on eviction suits therefore did not govern these premises. The court rejected the narrower interpretation in Punjab National Bank v. Sugan Chand, [1985] 1 A.R.C. 214, and held that reading down statutory language is inappropriate where it conflicts with the text and legislative history and does not produce an absurd, illogical, or unconstitutional result. The landlord had terminated the tenancy under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act.

rule.if: ordinary_eviction_suit and government_is_tenant and landlord_terminated_tenancy and leased_building_falls_within_broad_exemption and broad_exemption_regime_applies

predicates.ordinary_eviction_suit: The landlord brought an ordinary civil proceeding to recover possession from a tenant.
predicates.government_is_tenant: A government body occupied the building as a tenant.
predicates.landlord_terminated_tenancy: The landlord terminated the tenancy under the general law before seeking possession.
predicates.leased_building_falls_within_broad_exemp: The applicable definition treated a building leased by a government body as belonging to the exempt class of public buildings.
predicates.broad_exemption_regime_applies: The applicable legal regime exempted buildings in that defined class from rent-control protections.

issues.definition: When a landlord brings an ordinary eviction suit against a government tenant after terminating the tenancy, and the applicable regime exempts leased buildings of that kind, the landlord may seek possession by ordinary suit.

issues.legal_issue: A restriction on personal-occupation eviction by a public-body tenant does not require narrowing an otherwise broad definition of exempt public buildings.
material_facts: The statutory scheme included a special route allowing a landlord who had vacated a public building after ceasing public employment to seek possession for personal occupation.
The scheme also restricted use of that personal-occupation route against tenants that were government bodies, local authorities, or public corporations.
The court read the relevant provisions together and concluded that the restriction retained effect without narrowing the definition of public buildings.
issues.conclusion: The restriction on personal-occupation eviction did not make the broad definition redundant or justify limiting it; a landlord could not use that route against a government, local-authority, or public-corporation tenant.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 21(1), 21(1A), and 21(8) of the Uttar Pradesh Public Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, must be read together. Section 21(1A), notwithstanding the general exemption, provided a limited personal-occupation route for a landlord who had vacated a public building because public employment ended. Section 21(8) barred that route where the tenant was the government, a local authority, or a public-sector corporation. The omission of the referenced clauses from Explanation 1 did not prevent the provisions from being read harmoniously, and the restriction therefore did not render the broader definition in section 3(o) redundant.

rule.if: rent_control_scheme_interpretation and special_personal_occupation_route_exists and landlord_qualifies_for_special_route and tenant_is_public_body and personal_occupation_eviction_is_sought

predicates.rent_control_scheme_interpretation: The dispute concerns how provisions of a rent-control scheme operate together.
predicates.special_personal_occupation_route_exists: The scheme provides a special route for a landlord who vacated public accommodation after public employment ended to seek possession for personal occupation.
predicates.landlord_qualifies_for_special_route: The landlord vacated public accommodation because the landlord ceased to be employed by a public body.
predicates.tenant_is_public_body: The tenant is a government body, local authority, or public corporation.
predicates.personal_occupation_eviction_is_sought: The landlord seeks eviction on the ground of personal occupation.

issues.definition: When the special personal-occupation route is invoked by a qualifying landlord against a public-body tenant, that route is barred.
